items.stem: Data collected by the person who is going to use it is called
items.answer: primary data
items.markingKey: Primary data is first-hand; secondary data was collected by someone else.

items.stem: Explain why "How much TV do you watch?" is a poor survey question, and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: It is vague (no time period, no units) so answers cannot be compared. Better: "How many hours of TV did you watch yesterday? 0–1, 1–2, 2–3, more than 3".
items.markingKey: B1 vague / no time frame or response boxes; B1 improved question with time period and non-overlapping options [2]

items.stem: Explain why asking only students in the school basketball team is a biased way to find the favourite sport of students in a school.
items.answer: The sample is not representative: basketball players are much more likely to choose basketball.
items.markingKey: B1 not representative/biased; B1 reason [2]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) country of birth (b) the length of a leaf (c) the mass of a newborn baby
items.answer: (a) qualitative (b) continuous (c) continuous
items.markingKey: (a) B1 qualitative (b) B1 continuous (c) B1 continuous [3]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) the volume of water in a bottle (b) country of birth (c) type of transport used to get to school (d) favourite colour
items.answer: (a) continuous (b) qualitative (c) qualitative (d) qualitative
items.markingKey: (a) B1 continuous (b) B1 qualitative (c) B1 qualitative (d) B1 qualitative [4]

items.stem: Jonas is planning a statistical investigation to test the hypothesis: "Taller students have longer arm spans." (a) Describe how a suitable sample could be chosen and explain why it should be random. (b) Give one way the results could be displayed.
items.answer: (a) Choose a random sample (e.g. random numbers from a register) of a reasonable size, e.g. 50, from each relevant group so every member has an equal chance and bias is avoided. (b) A comparative bar chart
items.markingKey: (a) B1 random selection method; B1 reason (avoid bias) ; B1 size/groups [3] (b) B1 suitable display [1]

items.stem: Which of these is an example of secondary data?
options: Rainfall figures downloaded from a weather website
Answers to the student's own questionnaire
items.answer: Rainfall figures downloaded from a weather website
items.markingKey: It was collected by someone else.

items.stem: Explain the difference between discrete and continuous data, with an example of each.
items.answer: Discrete data can only take particular (often whole-number) values, e.g. number of children; continuous data can take any value in a range, e.g. height.
items.markingKey: B1 definitions; B1 correct examples [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a sample rather than a census.
items.answer: A sample is cheaper and quicker; but it may not represent the whole population, so results may be less accurate.
items.markingKey: B1 advantage; B1 disadvantage [2]

items.stem: Mei wants to find out about the average height of students in a school. Mei asks 30 people in the Year 11 classroom. Give two reasons why this sample may not give reliable results, and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: It is biased because older students are taller, so the sample is not representative of all ages; a sample of 30 is small. Improvement: choose a larger random sample from different places and times.
items.markingKey: B1 bias with reason; B1 sample size or single time/place; B1 sensible improvement (random/larger/varied) [3]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) shoe size (b) the time taken to run 100 m (c) favourite sport
items.answer: (a) discrete (b) continuous (c) qualitative
items.markingKey: (a) B1 discrete (b) B1 continuous (c) B1 qualitative [3]

items.stem: Tariq writes a questionnaire about the number of portions of fruit eaten yesterday. The response boxes are: less than 2, 2–5, 5 or more. Give two problems with these response boxes and write improved boxes.
items.answer: Problems: the value 5 belongs to two groups, and the groups are too wide to give much detail. Improved: 0, 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7 or more (whole numbers, no overlaps or gaps).
items.markingKey: B1 first problem; B1 second problem; B1 non-overlapping exhaustive boxes [3]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) the number of cars passing a school gate in an hour (b) the number of text messages sent in a day (c) the distance a ball is thrown
items.answer: (a) discrete (b) discrete (c) continuous
items.markingKey: (a) B1 discrete (b) B1 discrete (c) B1 continuous [3]

items.stem: Felix writes a questionnaire about the number of films watched last month. The response boxes are: 0–2, 2–4, 4–6. Give two problems with these response boxes and write improved boxes.
items.answer: Problems: the groups overlap (2 and 4 are in two groups) and there is no box for more than 6. Improved: 0, 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7 or more (whole numbers, no overlaps or gaps).
items.markingKey: B1 first problem; B1 second problem; B1 non-overlapping exhaustive boxes [3]

items.stem: Tomás is planning a statistical investigation to test the hypothesis: "Students in Year 9 spend more time on social media than students in Year 11." (a) Describe how a suitable sample could be chosen and explain why it should be random. (b) Give one way the results could be displayed.
items.answer: (a) Choose a random sample (e.g. random numbers from a register) of a reasonable size, e.g. 50, from each relevant group so every member has an equal chance and bias is avoided. (b) A pie chart for each group
items.markingKey: (a) B1 random selection method; B1 reason (avoid bias) ; B1 size/groups [3] (b) B1 suitable display [1]

items.stem: Elena is planning a statistical investigation to test the hypothesis: "Students in Year 9 spend more time on social media than students in Year 11." (a) State what data needs to be collected and whether it is discrete, continuous or qualitative. (b) Suggest how the data could be collected and whether it is primary or secondary data. (c) Give one way the results could be displayed.
items.answer: (a) Time spent on social media; continuous (b) A questionnaire/measurement by the student (primary) or published records (secondary), with a reason. (c) A pie chart for each group
items.markingKey: (a) B1 data; B1 type [2] (b) B1 method; B1 primary/secondary consistent [2] (c) B1 suitable display [1]

items.stem: Explain why the class intervals 10–20 and 20–30 are not suitable for recording heights of plants.
items.answer: A height of 20 cm would belong to both classes; use 10 ≤ h < 20 and 20 ≤ h < 30 instead.
items.markingKey: B1 overlapping at 20; B1 correct inequality notation [2]

items.stem: Explain one disadvantage of grouping data in a frequency table.
items.answer: The original individual values are lost, so exact statistics such as the mean or range cannot be found.
items.markingKey: B1 lose raw values; B1 consequence [2]

items.stem: A two-way table shows visitors and where they went, with some values missing. Local: Museum 30, Beach ?, Market 11, total 65; Tourist: Museum 22, Beach 13, Market ?, total 54; Total: Museum ?, Beach 37, Market 30, overall 119. Find the missing values.
items.answer: Total/Museum = 52; Local/Beach = 24; Tourist/Market = 19

items.answer: Total/Tennis = 25; Adults/total = 50; Adults/Swim = 22; Children/Gym = 13

A table that shows two sets of categories at once, such as gender and favourite subject, is called
items.answer: a two-way table
items.markingKey: Rows show one category and columns another.

items.stem: Explain how you can check that a completed two-way table is correct.
items.answer: The row totals and the column totals must both add up to the same grand total.
items.markingKey: B1 row totals; B1 column totals equal grand total [2]

items.stem: A two-way table shows students and how they travel to school. Explain why proportions are better than these numbers, and compare the groups using proportions.
items.answer: The groups are different sizes (62 and 65). Proportions: Boys 21/62 = 0.339, Girls 26/65 = 0.400, so Girls have the higher proportion.
items.markingKey: B1 different group sizes; M1 both proportions; A1 correct comparison [3]

items.stem: A two-way table shows members of a sports club and their favourite activity. items.markingKey: B1 different group sizes; M1 both proportions; A1 correct comparison [3]

items.stem: A two-way table shows customers at a café and their drink, with some values missing. Morning: Tea 17, Coffee ?, Juice 28, total 51; Afternoon: Tea 15, Coffee 25, Juice ?, total 50; Total: Tea ?, Coffee 31, Juice 38, overall 101. Find the missing values.

items.markingKey: B1 tallies correct for at least four values; B1 2 [2]

items.answer: A pie chart only shows proportions; a larger sector in one chart might represent fewer people if that chart shows a smaller total.

items.stem: Explain why a bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 50 instead of 0 can be misleading.
items.answer: The bars look much more different in height than the data really are, exaggerating differences.
items.markingKey: B1 axis not from 0; B1 exaggerates differences [2]

items.stem: The table shows the ways employees travel to work: Car 52, Train 15, Bus 4, Bicycle 49. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: Car 156°, Train 45°, Bus 12°, Bicycle 147°
items.markingKey: M1 360 ÷ 120 = 3° per item; A2 all angles correct (A1 for two) [3]

items.stem: A pie chart shows the favourite fruits of students. The sector for Mango has an angle of 232° and represents 29 people. Find the total number of people in the survey and the angle for a category containing 9 people.
items.answer: 45 people; 72°

items.stem: The maximum daily temperatures in Karachi for one week were: Mon 24 °C, Tue 25 °C, Wed 29 °C, Thu 22 °C, Fri 20 °C, Sat 25 °C, Sun 23 °C. The data are to be shown on a line graph. (a) State which variable goes on the horizontal axis and explain why. (b) Calculate the mean maximum temperature for the week, correct to 1 decimal place.
items.answer: (a) The day (time), because it is the independent variable and line graphs show change over time. (b) 24 °C

items.stem: In a pictogram, one symbol represents 8 cars. How many cars do 3½ symbols represent?
Explain why points on a line graph may be joined with straight lines.
items.answer: Joining shows the trend over time and allows an estimate of values between readings, assuming the change is steady between them.
items.markingKey: B1 shows trend; B1 estimate intermediate values [2]

items.stem: A survey of 120 people records the favourite fruits of students; 40 chose Apple. Mohammed draws a pie chart and uses an angle of 144° for Apple, by working out 40 × 3.6. Explain the mistake and find the correct angle.
items.answer: Multiplying by 3.6 only works when the total is 100. Each person is 360 ÷ 120 = 3°, so the angle is 40 × 3 = 120°.
items.markingKey: B1 total is 120, not 100; B1 120° [2]

items.stem: A survey of 30 people records the favourite fruits of students; 3 chose Orange. Mohammed draws a pie chart and uses an angle of 11° for Orange, by working out 3 × 3.6. Explain the mistake and find the correct angle.
items.answer: Multiplying by 3.6 only works when the total is 100. Each person is 360 ÷ 30 = 12°, so the angle is 3 × 12 = 36°.
items.markingKey: B1 total is 30, not 100; B1 36° [2]

items.stem: The table shows the types of tree in a park: Oak 15, Palm 14, Pine 6, Maple 10. Calculate the angle of each sector for a pie chart.
items.answer: Oak 120°, Palm 112°, Pine 48°, Maple 80°
items.markingKey: M1 360 ÷ 45 = 8° per item; A2 all angles correct (A1 for two) [3]

items.stem: A pie chart shows the favourite sports of club members. The sector for Basketball has an angle of 150° and represents 15 people. Find the total number of people in the survey and the angle for a category containing 3 people.

items.stem: The maximum daily temperatures in Lagos for one week were: Mon 21 °C, Tue 16 °C, Wed 15 °C, Thu 25 °C, Fri 23 °C, Sat 22 °C, Sun 19 °C. The data are to be shown on a line graph. (a) Find the largest increase from one day to the next, and say between which days it happened. (b) Explain why a line graph is more suitable than a pie chart for these data.
items.answer: (a) 10 °C, from Wed to Thu (b) The data show change over time; a pie chart shows parts of a whole, and the temperatures are not parts of a total.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 differences; A1 10 °C Wed–Thu [2] (b) B1 change over time; B1 not parts of a whole [2]

items.stem: The maximum daily temperatures in Auckland for one week were: Mon 17 °C, Tue 21 °C, Wed 25 °C, Thu 22 °C, Fri 25 °C, Sat 25 °C, Sun 25 °C. The data are to be shown on a line graph. (c) Calculate the mean maximum temperature for the week, correct to 1 decimal place.
items.answer: (a) The day (time), because it is the independent variable and line graphs show change over time. (b) 4 °C, from Tue to Wed (c) 22.9 °C
items.markingKey: (a) B1 day; B1 reason [2] (b) M1 differences; A1 4 °C Tue–Wed [2] (c) M1 160 ÷ 7; A1 22.9 [2]

items.stem: In a stem-and-leaf diagram with key 3 | 4 = 34, what value does 5 | 7 represent?
items.markingKey: Stem 5 (tens), leaf 7 (units).

items.stem: Why must a stem-and-leaf diagram have a key?
options: To show what the stems and leaves represent
items.answer: To show what the stems and leaves represent
items.markingKey: For example 3 | 4 could mean 34 or 3.4.

items.stem: Explain one advantage of a stem-and-leaf diagram over a grouped frequency table.
items.answer: It keeps the original data values, so the median, mode and range can be found exactly, while still showing the shape of the distribution.
items.markingKey: B1 keeps raw data; B1 exact statistics/shape [2]

items.stem: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows the test marks (marks): 3 | 0 1 2 2 5 5 ; 4 | 4 ; 5 | 3 3 4 ; 6 | 2 (key: 3 | 3 = 33 marks). Find the range and the median.
items.answer: range 32 marks; median 35 marks
items.markingKey: B1 range 62 − 30 = 32; M1 (11 + 1) ÷ 2 = 6th value; A1 median 35 [3]

items.stem: Tomás's class and Kenji's class each recorded their numbers of push-ups in one minute. Tomás's class: 4 | 0 1 2 2 3 ; 5 | 6 9 ; 6 | 5 7 ; 7 | 2 5 8 9. Kenji's class: 4 | 9 ; 5 | 1 1 3 3 ; 6 | 2 4 7 8 ; 7 | 2 5 ; 8 | 1 4. Key for both: 3 | 4 = 34. (a) Find the median for each class. (b) Name a display that would show both sets of data on one diagram while keeping every value.
items.answer: (a) Tomás: 59; Kenji: 64 (b) A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram
items.markingKey: (a) B1 59; B1 64 [2] (b) B1 back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram [1]

items.stem: Which is the most appropriate display for showing how the population of a town changed every year from 2010 to 2024?

items.stem: Explain why a stem-and-leaf diagram is not suitable for showing the favourite colours of a class.

items.stem: Sipho records these values: 27, 41, 25, 54, 59, 26, 44, 45, 32, 38, 38, 47, 52, 20, 54. Sipho says the median is 45 because it is the middle value of the list. Explain the error and use an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram to find the correct median.
items.answer: The values must be put in order first. Ordered diagram: 2 | 0 5 6 7 ; 3 | 2 8 8 ; 4 | 1 4 5 7 ; 5 | 2 4 4 9 (key 2 | 3 = 23). The median is the 8th value, 41.

items.stem: Elena's class and Priya's class each recorded their numbers of push-ups in one minute. Elena's class: 3 | 0 4 ; 4 | 0 5 8 ; 5 | 0 2 4 7 8 8 8 ; 6 | 2. items.markingKey: M1 360 ÷ 40 = 9° per item; A2 all angles correct (A1 for two) [3]

items.stem: A pie chart shows the favourite sports of club members. The sector for Tennis has an angle of 30° and represents 2 people. Find the total number of people in the survey and the angle for a category containing 3 people.
items.answer: 24 people; 45°

items.stem: The maximum daily temperatures in Lisbon for one week were: Mon 23 °C, Tue 20 °C, Wed 26 °C, Thu 22 °C, Fri 23 °C, Sat 20 °C, Sun 21 °C. The data are to be shown on a line graph. (a) State which variable goes on the horizontal axis and explain why. (b) Calculate the mean maximum temperature for the week, correct to 1 decimal place.
items.answer: (a) The day (time), because it is the independent variable and line graphs show change over time. (b) 22.1 °C

items.stem: Explain how to find the median from an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram with 25 values.
items.answer: The median is the 13th value ((25 + 1) ÷ 2); count along the leaves from the smallest value to the 13th.
items.markingKey: B1 13th value; B1 count from the smallest [2]

items.stem: Amara records these values: 56, 47, 51, 29, 31, 50, 47, 30, 21, 27, 29, 35, 38. Amara says the median is 47 because it is the middle value of the list. Explain the error and use an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram to find the correct median.
items.answer: The values must be put in order first. Ordered diagram: 2 | 1 7 9 9 ; 3 | 0 1 5 8 ; 4 | 7 7 ; 5 | 0 1 6 (key 2 | 3 = 23). The median is the 7th value, 35.
items.markingKey: B1 data not ordered; B1 ordered diagram; B1 median 35 [3]

items.stem: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows the test marks (marks): 4 | 0 1 1 3 6 ; 5 | 8 9 ; 6 | 1 1 9 ; 7 | 5 (key: 4 | 3 = 43 marks). Find the range and the median.
items.answer: range 35 marks; median 58 marks
items.markingKey: B1 range 75 − 40 = 35; M1 (11 + 1) ÷ 2 = 6th value; A1 median 58 [3]

items.stem: Felix's class and Arjun's class each recorded their times in seconds to complete an obstacle course. Felix's class: 4 | 1 ; 5 | 0 1 3 9 9 ; 6 | 0 1 1 4 6 6 ; 7 | 6 9 9. Arjun's class: 2 | 7 9 ; 3 | 1 2 8 ; 4 | 2 3 7 ; 5 | 1 2 7 ; 6 | 1 1 5 ; 7 | 5. Key for both: 3 | 4 = 34. (a) Find the median for each class. (b) Find the range for each class. (c) Name a display that would show both sets of data on one diagram while keeping every value.
items.answer: (a) Felix: 61; Arjun: 47 (b) Felix: 38; Arjun: 48 (c) A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram
items.markingKey: (a) B1 61; B1 47 [2] (b) B1 38; B1 48 [2] (c) B1 back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram [1]

items.stem: Data described in words rather than numbers is called
items.answer: qualitative (categorical)
items.markingKey: Examples: colours, types of food.

items.stem: Ethan wants to find out about how much exercise adults do each week. Ethan asks 50 people outside a gym. Give two reasons why this sample may not give reliable results, and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: It is biased because people at a gym are likely to exercise more than average; a sample of 50 is small. Improvement: choose a larger random sample from different places and times.
items.markingKey: B1 bias with reason; B1 sample size or single time/place; B1 sensible improvement (random/larger/varied) [3]

items.stem: Hana wants to find out about the favourite type of music of people in a city. Hana asks 30 people at a classical concert. Give two reasons why this sample may not give reliable results, and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: It is biased because concert-goers will over-represent classical music; a sample of 30 is small. Improvement: choose a larger random sample from different places and times.
items.markingKey: B1 bias with reason; B1 sample size or single time/place; B1 sensible improvement (random/larger/varied) [3]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) eye colour (b) the temperature at noon (c) the volume of water in a bottle
items.answer: (a) qualitative (b) continuous (c) continuous
items.markingKey: (a) B1 qualitative (b) B1 continuous (c) B1 continuous [3]

items.stem: Classify each of these types of data as discrete, continuous or qualitative. (a) the number of cars passing a school gate in an hour (b) the temperature at noon (c) country of birth (d) eye colour
items.answer: (a) discrete (b) continuous (c) qualitative (d) qualitative
items.markingKey: (a) B1 discrete (b) B1 continuous (c) B1 qualitative (d) B1 qualitative [4]

items.stem: Kenji is planning a statistical investigation to test the hypothesis: "Taller students have longer arm spans." (a) State what data needs to be collected and whether it is discrete, continuous or qualitative. (b) Describe how a suitable sample could be chosen and explain why it should be random. (c) Give one way the results could be displayed.
items.answer: (a) Height and arm span; continuous (b) Choose a random sample (e.g. random numbers from a register) of a reasonable size, e.g. 50, from each relevant group so every member has an equal chance and bias is avoided. (c) A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram
items.markingKey: (a) B1 data; B1 type [2] (b) B1 random selection method; B1 reason (avoid bias) ; B1 size/groups [3] (c) B1 suitable display [1]

items.stem: Why are grouped frequency tables used for continuous data?
options: Because continuous data has no mode
There are too many different values to list individually
items.answer: There are too many different values to list individually
items.markingKey: Grouping into class intervals summarises the data.

items.stem: A two-way table shows visitors and where they went. Local: Museum 13, Beach 8, Market 29, total 50; Tourist: Museum 8, Beach 29, Market 10, total 47; Total: Museum 21, Beach 37, Market 39, overall 97. Lina compares the groups using the numbers who chose Beach (8 and 29). Explain why proportions are better than these numbers, and compare the groups using proportions.
items.answer: The groups are different sizes (50 and 47). Proportions: Local 8/50 = 0.160, Tourist 29/47 = 0.617, so Tourist have the higher proportion.
items.markingKey: B1 different group sizes; M1 both proportions; A1 correct comparison [3]

items.stem: Here are data showing the number of eggs laid each day by a hen house: 5, 2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 3, 5, 3, 5, 4, 1, 0, 2. Complete a frequency table for the values 0 to 5 and write down the frequency of 5.
items.markingKey: B1 tallies correct for at least four values; B1 3 [2]

items.stem: A two-way table shows students and how they travel to school, with some values missing. Boys: Walk 19, Bus ?, Car 23, total 56; Girls: Walk 30, Bus 20, Car ?, total 65; Total: Walk ?, Bus 34, Car 38, overall 121. Find the missing values.
items.answer: Total/Walk = 49; Boys/Bus = 14; Girls/Car = 15
items.markingKey: B1 for each correct missing value, using row/column totals [3]

items.stem: A two-way table shows students and how they travel to school. Some values are missing. Boys: Walk 12, Bus 21, Car ?, total 62; Girls: Walk ?, Bus 6, Car 25, total 47; Total: Walk 28, Bus ?, Car 54, overall 109. (a) Find the number in the group Boys who chose Car. (b) Find the number in the group Girls who chose Walk. (c) One person from the group Girls is chosen at random. Find the probability that they chose Car.
Answer both parts. (a) Which type of graph is best for showing how a temperature changes over a day? (b) In a pie chart showing 60 people, how many degrees represent one person?
items.answer: (a) A line graph (b) 6°
items.markingKey: (a) Line graphs show change over time. (b) 360 ÷ 60 = 6°.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a pie chart cannot be used to compare the actual numbers in two groups of different sizes. (b) Explain why points on a line graph may be joined with straight lines.
items.answer: (a) A pie chart only shows proportions; a larger sector in one chart might represent fewer people if that chart shows a smaller total. (b) Joining shows the trend over time and allows an estimate of values between readings, assuming the change is steady between them.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 shows proportions; B1 totals differ [2] (b) B1 shows trend; B1 estimate intermediate values [2]
